He was best man several times and father of the bride at least once. We said goodbye to our friends in the RCR before they went off to Valcartier to join the rest of the Regiment. The death of my mother and attendant obligations took up quite a bit of time. There were quite a few parties and a sort of eve of Waterloo gaiety. People like Johny Birmingham telephoned begging F to get him into the Fd Coy. This was "Schmid's" pigeon not F's.

I think F was very happy at this time doing a job he liked, one they had been training for for years. Later we heard that Gen McNaughton questioned F's appointment as OC FD Coy, he had heard "that Henshaw was drinking a lot". Both Schmidlin and Charlie Hertzberg (RIP) assured Andy that F wouldn't let him and First Div down and he didn't. So word came that he was to revert to major and go overseas in command of the First of the Field.

The advance party First Div sailed away, Des McGee with them. We were left with his Buick and Neel Hodson's as well as our Chev. Our place looked like a used car lot. The 1st and 2nd Contingents of first div left. We spent a quiet family Christmas.

The day of embarkation arrived and the Field Coy marched through the streets to the docks; the "little wives" and I drove from corner to corner to catch every possible glimpse of them without actually marching alongside, holding hands and clinging as the Halifax kin of the sappers did. Tommy Williams went about taking pictures.
F very kindly let the little wives have their husbands ashore till the very last minute. He and the wifeless did their work.
On the Sunday Barb and the boys came down to have a last glimpse of their Daddy but he didn't appear — obviously he was much too busy to be hanging over the side of the ship nattering to his family.

A friend in the know told me the ETD and once more the little wives and I hot footed it down to the dock. The girls soon found their men and Jean and George had a ship to shore conversation almost within touching distance. Sappers leaning over the rail in the bow said I'd find F at the stern, but there I was told he'd be midships, near Spencer. But he didn't appear and I wasn't too sad because I was counting on meeting him in London within two weeks. When we met in London he explained his non appearance when they sailed—their departure coincided with the opening of the bar which he could not miss!!

The Fd Coy went to [name uncertain: Talaferra] Barracks on arrival at Aldershot. It was still pretty miserably cold, but the worst of the winter was over when the plumbing didn't work and the tiny fires were quite inadequate to heat the big rooms of the Barracks. There was five day landing leave and F came to London and joined me at the Cumberland Hotel. I half expected him to want to tear up to Scotland to do a walking tour, but he was contented to stay and frivol in London Town. This we did with the Lutons, Penhales, Chris Vokes, Pat Kelly, Steve Morres and Janet Carruthers; the latter was joining the MTC and brought her uniform for our inspection, khaki cotton stockings, shirts, ties, and even khaki underwear. Her jackets and skirts were being made to order by Paquin!!! F suggested that I try to join the MTC too but I pointed out that I had deserted my children in order to be with him in England and not to pursue a war career of my own.

Back at Aldershot I stayed in the quaint Victoria Hotel. A large blackboard in the hall listed room numbers, alongside of which occupants chalked their breakfast orders. We saw old friends and went to some mess parties. At the RCR we met Dorothy Albrecht; when F was presented to her she exclaimed "Oh you are the man who eats dog food." It was true for one day when F arrived at the Cottage at Petawawa, hungry, he found an inviting looking dish of what he thought was cooked hamburg; he made and ate a substantial sandwich and pronounced it damn good.

Dorothy very quickly proved herself a true friend to Canadians. Not very long after this she had the Sprys, Mathers, F and I, as well as her son and herself staying in her house, as well as the two known as GusanNeel, Taschereau and Hodson (RCR).

The Coy moved to Pangbourne for river training and were quartered in one of the larger stately homes in a beautiful park. Basildon Park and Hall belonged to the Ferdenandez family. Father and mother were living in the Dower House, ugly and small but cosy and they gave us a beautiful dinner there. Their son and daughter in law, Sally, a deep-south youall American, lived in a converted stable within the brickwalled kitchen gardens. They were very friendly and gave a wonderful cocktail party in another of their houses, a ranch type beautifully furnished one, which was closed for the duration.

Back in Aldershot again at Talaferra we took a small cottage at Cove with the Aitkens. Bob was due to go to France almost at once so he and Nell rated the double bedded master bedroom with fireplace. After Bob left Nell was pretty sad and twitchy. One morning, about 6 a.m. F's driver decided to wash the windows of the station wagon and as each window was finished he banged the door shut. Nell stood three windows and then leant from her casement window and in a scathing tone (her very very scathing) said "IF you have to wash your car at this hour of the morning please do it under some other window."

ENGLAND in 1940
The Dagger Thrust at the Heart of Berlin

About the first day of May the balloon went up for the First Field Coy. They were ordered to proceed to what one of the NCO's assured me was Southampton—but for South read North; they were to embus at midnight and the evening was spent in the officers' quarters, where F allowed the little wives to spend all the available time with their husbands. Long before zero hour we began to harness F into his kit, and it took the combined efforts of his batman, driver adjutant and me to hoist him into the front seat of his lorry once he was fully laden; then he couldn't raise his arm to look at his watch to synchronize time of departure. An appended letter from F. tells how they got lost following what they thought was the convoy's tail. What he didn't mention was the rage of the RAF OC of the airfield in the middle of which they found themselves, come the cold grey dawn.

A report of an accident to a cyclist of the Hasty P's which was received at Red Cross Headquarters in London, where I was presently working, plus a telephone call from F when the operator told me quite plainly that the call came from Kettering, jelled my decision to become a camp follower. So getting leave from Mrs. H I dashed to Swan & Edgar, bought blouse and coat and skirt, tie and a sort of uniform hat, all navy blue including stockings. Up Regent street at [unclear] blue oxfords were obtained. All in all a creditable uniform. Then a mad dash to Paddington where I was surprised to find Mary Plow and Rosamund Crowe and a spaniel dog as fellow passengers. They were going to stay with friends but I was on my own to find a place to stay as well as finding Freddie. I bused from Northampton and got out at a village where I saw some Signallers stringing wire. They directed me to the Field Coy where I got a lift and went to visit the Hasty P in hospital not far away. He was still unconscious but the staff were very glad to have me go to his company and get his papers, which had not yet arrived. When Freddie had some free time we went across the road to a little pub where we had dinner and I stayed the night; but since F could have very little time off I went back to London early the next morning and back to Berkeley Square to work. I was given quite a bit of praise for my efforts on behalf of the Hasty P. I heard later that General McNaughton was furious when he spotted a group of wives congregated on a street corner in a nearby village.

On May 24th the Fd. Coy went off on the "Bust to Brest". As the train pulled out of the station [name uncertain: Daughinee], "Daugh", leaned from a window and called out to me "Well Mrs. Henshaw we always leave on the 24th of May and I hope we'll all get back safely as we've done before." They did that time. Mary Plow telephoned to say they were coming back and I'm afraid my reply led her to believe I wasn't too pleased; it wasn't that I didn't want F back again I just felt sad for them that they had to come running home with their tails between their legs. Frustrating. Connelly also phoned to tell me they were going to Bourassa Barracks instead of back to Tal---- He also told me the ETA of the train so Dorothy and [unclear] Bell hied us down to Farnborough station in the cold grey dawn and were there when the train crept in. Not a sign of life at first then a few sleepy looking soldiers peered out the windows. Capt. Bell, RCR Medical officer descended and wrapped his wife in the all time record of public hugging and kissing. Soon troops were detraining and I was able to tell F of Connelly's message; the RTO hadn't word of it and told them to go to Tal. but when they did some phoning they discovered the truth and so the Coy. had a much shorter march to make and at the end found a hot meal awaiting. I preened, but heard later that Bill Hodson, OC [unclear], not too well, disgruntled and unhappy, seeing three females on the platform said to his son Neel, one of his Coy officers, "These women anything to do with you?" The RCR went to a rather unpleasant camp site but they still came to D's in Farnborough for succor (drink and food and female company!!). D & Gus and F and I had a braw day in London when they went to order new kit; for all they owned except what they were wearing was left behind in France. I always regretted F's beautiful blue silk pyjamas and the blue soup cups I had presented to the Fd Coy mess had to fall into the German hands.

When F arrived back from England in July 1941 there was no job ready for him at the College; he was given a desk in [name uncertain: Archie Campbell]'s office and began to do some work for Col Lowther on the Senior Officers Classes. Colonel Lowther was transferred and FRH became OC of the Course, running nine successful courses, until he was retired in June 1943. He had a grand lot of instructors to work with and I believe he had a very happy time during the year and a half or a bit more that he was at the College.

Undoubtedly his friends, Hertzberg, Commandant RMC and Stuart, Chief of Staff, were instrumental in getting FRH this very pleasant job. It included a very fine quarter at the College to which the family moved in the spring of '42. Previously we lived in a small unfireplaced flat on Johnston Street, adequate but not very cosy. Barbara went to Sydenham School that year. Helen came home in April, just after the move to RMC, which was a good thing as she brought two college pals and as RMC was still functioning as a cadet college there were lads to entertain the glamour pusses.

The circumstances surrounding Helen's meeting with Jim Hunter always seem most romantic; Jim was learning to fly at Collins Bay. FRH had played a good deal of chess with Vaughan Morris RAF coming back in the ship; this officer was coming out to be adjutant at Collins Bay, an Empire training station for the Fleet Air Arm and Air Force. They renewed acquaintance at the RMC boxing tournament and eventually gravitated back to quarters. There was to be an Engineer Womens' Auxiliary dance we were sponsoring and the girls needed escorts so Vaughan agreed to provide same. The girls expected bell-bottom trousers but to their surprise a party of subs arrived — all rather short except one — Helen chose him. Next day, he and two friends were paddling under the causeway just as the girls were on their way to town, greetings were exchanged and later they "just happened to meet" in the popular eating place, Green Room. Helen phoned to ask permission to invite them for supper which of course was granted and so that was the first meeting of Helen and Jim. The other lad was Ray Oakes, Jim's pal.

Fortunately there was an adequate meal in preparation, we generally seemed to eat well in those days and usually had people to help in the kitchen. This was made possible by a plan worked out by Mary Dalton. In return for room and board a wife and one or two small children, or none at all, gave her services in the household while the husband was stationed in Kingston, either at Vimy or some other Barracks. We were lucky to have Margaret and Leo Dupuis during the time he was in Kingston with the RCME. We had one frightful scare during their residence when the younger baby fell into a very boiling hot bath and got quite badly burned and had to be hurried to hospital. But he was a rugged type and survived. One night, later on, Helen, hurrying in to fetch the carrots crashed through the glass part of the pantry door and cut her hands and ruined the carrots — with butter on too. Leo got into a jam at the end, Margaret went home with the kids just before he was due to leave with a draft for overseas. His last night he got mixed up in a party and overslept and missed his train. I never saw a sadder young soldier than poor Leo sitting in the kitchen writing an explanatory letter to his wife. I have never heard anything of them since.

To return to the Hunter-Henshaw courtship. It had the approval of her parents and as he was of sufficient rank and seniority for permission to marry to be a mere formality, or perhaps that was because it was in the War, in any case, they were very soon affianced. It was very funny when Jim asked Pop for Helen's hand. Pop said, "let's have a drink" and then suggested going out to acquaint the females that the seal of approval had been placed on the engagement. In the garden they found the bride to be swinging like a monkey on a heavy rope attached to a large branch high up in the huge tree, of course with A ROPE not her tail. So plans were made for an early wedding and it was decided to have it in Como. There were splendid pictures taken to tell the rest of the story.

F looked particularly smart at the wedding in blue patrol jacket.

On May 19th 1944 we moved into Riversmead and it was undoubtedly a most thrilling moment, being the first time we had a home of our very own since 1923 when we left Wavertree Farm in Nova Scotia. The house was full of places to investigate, bound to fire the imaginations of the two teen agers we had at home, George and Barb. Cousin Edna had left a substantial amount of furniture behind, beds, bureaus, tables, kitchen cupboard and above all two almirahs (wardrobes). But there were some alterations necessary and these were carried out during the early years of our occupancy. We acquired three bathrooms and a wonderful back porch, a supposedly ratproof cellar space and the railing from the lower gallery was taken away. Grapevine gradually disappeared and odd flower beds and shrubs dotted about the lawns were turned into lawn and the flowers confined into border beds of rectangular shape. There was a wonderful place for vegetables, especially early. One year we were eating green peas etc on June 1st, having planted same on April 15th. Gradually the kitchen garden took shape and is now a lovely place; at one stage it definitely got too large, it defied the instructions "Never plant more garden than your wife can take care of". Raspberry canes flourished and the crop was terrific; it is supposed that one can clear a thousand dollars an acre from the berries. Perhaps we will reach that stage one day.

At a birthday party that Jim Hunter gave for his wife in Halifax at the L.N Hotel two of the guests said they were coming to Mtl to spend their leave, so Helen suggested that they come to Como for a weekend, where the rule was open house, particularly for service personnel. Jim Hunter said "you'll love it, she's mad and he drinks".

When Paul and Barbara got married the RC Church didn't allow the ceremony to take place in the church proper if one of the contracting parties was non RC. So Pop always claimed that Barbara was not well and truly married since the wedding took place in the Priest's house. Father Cloutier did everything possible to make it a happy occasion and arranged to have his curate play and sing "Oh Promise Me", in English — this curate was very much a tenor. The reception this time was at Riversmead, attended by Paul's Family and Barb's, which then included Aunt Ruth and Grandfather. [name uncertain: Ancy Gundry] was then a staunch helper on any and all occasions. (Even to celebrating Mousa's birthday with her, Pop and to quote Grandfather "a girl called Jean Cote") There was real Fizz and thunder flashes, laid on by Freddie, who happened to be here and busy getting in love with Naomi Ritchie.

It seems unnecessary to go over the details of Freddie's illness and to describe the treatments carried out. In hospital for two months, in great discomfort if not actual pain, he displayed great courage, self discipline and consideration for others that were characteristics of his amiable nature. From his return to Riversmead, on March 4th, until his death at the end of August, weekly visits were made to the test centre at the Montreal General Hospital, where the staff were most considerate and kindly. It seems somewhat sad to think that on his last trip to the hospital, on a very hot day, Tuesday August 18th, wanting a refreshing drink of either gin & orange or plain orange juice, they refused to serve him in the car and of course he wasn't up to going into the restaurant. He had been a spending customer there for years.

The funeral took place on Wednesday 26th (Small Paul's birthday) and burial was in St. Mary's churchyard. It was impossible to carry out his wish to be buried up the farm; it required a special license which had to be applied for from Quebec. But through the great efforts of Moser and David the kind of coffin he had requested was made in time. Quite a few Sapper friends came from Ottawa, Kingston and Montreal.

The Brunet Company made a very fine headstone, their one mistake being to make a stroke instead of a dot between Lieut and Col. The Engineer crest was very well done, the workman is evidently an artist. A brass memorial tablet was dedicated on Dec. 13th (his birthday) and placed on the window ledge below the Henshaw Memorial window.
No. 801 Lieutenant-Colonel Frederick Robert Henshaw M.C., psc, R.C.E. (Ret'd)

Lt.-Col. F. R. Henshaw was born in Montreal in 1890 and was educated at R.M.C. from which he graduated in 1911. He spent two years at the R.S.M.C., Chatham, England. He served overseas from 1915 to 1919 and on his return to Canada became a farmer in Nova Scotia. In 1923 he was invited to rejoin the Permanent Force and served with the Royal Canadian Engineers until he went to the Staff College in Quetta, Baluchistan. In 1929 he was Assistant Director of Military Intelligence and Editor of the Defence Quarterly. Later, while District Engineer Officer in Kingston Ontario, he, with the late Colonel "Bill" Wilgar and others, was instrumental in carrying out a re-organization of the Corps, which resulted in better training for Militia Engineers.

Lt. Col Henshaw reverted to Major in order to go overseas in command of the 1st Field Company, took part in the famous "Bust to Brest" and was subsequently promoted to Lt. Col. Returning to Canada in 1941, Lt. Col. Henshaw was posted to R.M.C., where he was in charge of the Senior Officers' Courses until 1943. He retired in that year and again became a farmer at Riversmead, Como P. Que. He died on 23 August 1959, at Como and is survived by his widow, the former Helen Graham, two sons and two daughters.

The death of Fred Carson in Montreal on May 3rd 1960 brings many memories to mind of an association of the Carson and Henshaw families over the years. Freddie told me that he determined to join the Army after seeing Fred, home on leave from the REs, riding on the Lower Common in Kingston. Freddie wanted to join British Infantry, but Ken Stuart, one of his classmates, persuaded him, among others, to try for Canadian Engineers. They were accepted, for which I have always thanked God, because, had Freddie become a BBI he would undoubtedly have been killed early on in the First War, before his group of CEs got overseas. (They were kept on and on in Canada doing defences and training until Artie Lawson, who had camped on the steps of NDHQ, got them started overseas.) Without Freddie, none of my lovely and intelligent children and grandchildren would have been born!!

Doss and I had female babies, Pat and Barbara, in Kingston General Hospital, on practically the same day; the girls met again when we came back to Kingston in 1941 when they were classmates at Sydenham School. By the time Peter left RMC to join the REs in 1942, Doss and I were working at the Blood Clinic, where she did a wonderful job. She must have been under a terrific strain, with Fred in the East and the three boys somewhere abroad.

During the summer of 1942 George Henshaw, 14, delivered groceries for a shop on Barrie Street and sometimes was delivering Lady Carson's order at the back door as his mother arrived at the front for tea.

I have been told that before Doss died in 1944, when Fred had come back and they had some happy time together, that she regained much of her earlier beauty and gaiety. Freddie once told me that Dorothy Brownfield was the prettiest girl at her coming-out June Ball.

When Fred came to live in Montreal, with his sister Vera and Pat and the ever faithful Nanna, we used to see him fairly often, dining with him or having him for Sunday lunch at Riversmead, with such of his family as were about. We had one classic day when Fred and Nadine came out for Hunt races, but latterly our meetings seemed to be confined to chance encounters in banks, airports, railway station and clubs. The last time Fred and Freddie and I were together was in '57 at the RMC Reunion. Now they are both gone, two very gallant Sapper soldiers.

leg.how: Canadian Pacific liner Empress of Canada, first class
leg.note: The Hong Kong Daily Press lists “Major and Mrs. F. R. Henshaw and three children” among the Empress of Canada’s departures for Vancouver on 15 February. The Canadian passenger list names Frederick, Helen, their daughter and both Quetta-born sons. The Daily Colonist gives the ship’s voyage as from Manila, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Yokohama; the timetable put her at Shanghai on 18 February and Yokohama on 24 February. Those are the ship’s calls, not stops the family is known to have made.

early-years.label: A family manuscript
early-years.text: Helen writes across several generations. Letters from Frederick’s mother and grandparents sit alongside her own recollections. The original pages remain available to read beside the transcription.

glace-bay-school.label: A changing world
glace-bay-school.text: The family’s Glace Bay years overlap with Marconi’s wireless experiments. The letters describe visits and five o’clock tea: an invention becoming part of everyday family life.

Marconi’s Glace Bay receiving room, 17 October 1907

rmc-1908.label: No. 801
rmc-1908.text: Helen records his entry to RMC in 1908 and graduation in 1911. The number follows him into the obituary reproduced near the end of the biography.

halifax-1913.label: In the public record
halifax-1913.text: The London Gazette of June 4, 1917 names Lieutenant Frederick Robert Henshaw, Engineers, in the Military Cross list. The announcement records the honour; it does not supply a citation describing a particular action.

links.title: His First World War service file (LAC)

wavertree.label: A shared life
wavertree.text: A farm, an early-morning wedding, a runaway kitten: the scale of this account is often domestic. Helen’s humour is part of the history.

quetta.label: Three generations, one place
quetta.text: Steamships and trains carried the family east to Quetta. Freddie was born there in 1926; George’s 1927 birth is family-confirmed. The Indian Army List names Major Henshaw among the 1926 students. The homeward passage is now documented: Singapore in late January 1928, then the Empress of Canada from Hong Kong to Victoria.

links.title: Indian Army List, January 1927, p. 885 (Staff College students, 1926)

ottawa.label: Found in the officers’ list
ottawa.text: The Department of National Defence list for July 1928 names him “Assistant Director of Military Intelligence,” dated 1 January 1928. Helen used the same title. The family recalls a separate record using “deputy director”; that record has not been found.

camping.label: The article, identified
camping.text: Helen refers to Frederick’s “To Ontario’s Sea Coast by Canoe” in the Defence Quarterly. It appeared in the Canadian Defence Quarterly for January 1931, pages 255–263. The full article is not among the scanned pages.

rmc-war.label: Retirement in wartime?
rmc-war.text: Helen’s manuscript says he was retired in June 1943. The RMC Review confirms he directed the Senior Officers’ Course from April 1942, but the retirement date itself is still unverified: a search of the 1943 and early 1944 Canada Gazette army lists found no notice, though that search was incomplete. His Second World War service file, which can be requested from Library and Archives Canada, should settle it.

links.title: The college in an archival view, [1937?]

riversmead.label: Inheritance and homecoming
riversmead.text: The family remembers an inheritance in the 1930s. Helen dates the move into Riversmead precisely: May 19, 1944. Ownership and taking up residence are different events.

links.title: Riversmead in Greenwood’s family history (photograph undated)

carson.label: Memory after a life
carson.text: This final remembrance is dated 1960, after Frederick’s death. Elsewhere Helen cites a school visit in November 1961. The biography gathered later recollections as well as older letters.

wartime.title: Overseas in the First World War.
wartime.description: Helen leaves these years for letters she meant to quote. The service records recover a fuller outline: training and command in England, two periods in the France and Belgium theatre, and a return to Canada in June 1919.
wartime.caption: Helen’s promised letters are not in the scanned set. The added markers come from the service file: Boulogne is a recorded departure; Nice is a leave entry. “France and Belgium” is the official combined theatre label, not a reconstructed battle itinerary. The map draws no wartime route.

regions.name: France
regions.subtitle: Helen’s unfinished account
regions.note: Helen mentions letters written from France. Their dates and locations are not supplied in this scanned account.

legs.note: Helen credits Artie Lawson with getting the trained engineers sent overseas. His file records his appointment as assistant instructor at the Canadian Engineers Training Depot from 29 April 1915.
A week in France, returning from Boulogne on 26 August 1915.

legs.how: Adjutant, 3rd Divisional Engineers; later 7th Field Company
legs.note: The 1925 Militia List records service in the combined France and Belgium theatre from 25 March 1916 to 18 March 1917, then again from 16 March 1918 to 6 May 1919. Between those periods he commanded the 14th Field Company in England; in 1918 he joined the 12th Battalion, Canadian Engineers.
The file reads “Sailed Canada 6.6.19” and “Olympic 12/6/19”; the Olympic was then trooping between Southampton and Halifax.

wartime.title: Training in England. An expedition to France.
wartime.description: Helen’s account follows the Field Company through English training grounds, their time together around Aldershot, and the company’s return from France. These maps separate his named locations from the clues in her own journeys.
wartime.caption: Markers identify approximate places named in Helen’s recollection, not a reconstructed military itinerary. The engineer headquarters war diary dates the company’s Pangbourne training to March 1940, the move north to 30 May and the Brittany expedition to 8–15 June 1940; its party landed at Brest on 14 June and was recalled the same day. Frederick is not named in those June pages.

legs.how: Third Flight, convoy TC 3 (liner not identified)
legs.note: The 1st Field Company crossed with the Third Flight; it was not yet in England on 24 January. Stacey dates the Third Flight’s sailing to 30 January and disembarkation to 8–9 February; this does not supply one exact Clyde arrival day or identify Henshaw’s liner.

sources.title: C. P. Stacey, Six Years of War

legs.note: “The 1st. FD. COY. … arrived and proceeded to their quarters in TALAVERA … BKS.”
Major Henshaw visited Wallingford and Pangbourne beforehand, on 1 March.
The force for Calais and Dunkirk was recalled before sailing.
Helen remembered this as the first of May.

legs.how: Ville d’Alger out; Port Montreal back
legs.note: Transport left for Falmouth and Brest on 8 June; the party landed at Brest on 14 June, was recalled that evening and anchored at Falmouth on 15 June. Frederick is not named in these pages.
Helen followed the company and expected to meet Frederick in London within two weeks.
He played chess on the voyage with Vaughan Morris of the RAF. The battalion diary records his transfer and a farewell for Frederick and Helen on 4 July 1941, but not the sailing date or ship.

Croil traces his role in the river service back to acquiring Oldfield in 1846; the earlier enterprise and the later company should not be collapsed into a single founding date.

records.title: Ruth’s birth year
records.text: Helen gives 31 March 1894. Ruth’s headstone on the Henshaw monument at Mount Royal Cemetery reads 31 March 1895. An April 1895 letter from Grandfather Shepherd congratulating Beatrice on a daughter also points to 1895. Helen’s date is kept as she wrote it. A baptism record would settle the question.

links.title: Ruth Beatrice Henshaw, Find a Grave memorial (headstone photograph)

records.title: The messages across the Atlantic
records.text:
Beatrice’s letter of 22 December 1902 reports Mr Vyvyan’s telephone call about two messages sent “yesterday morning.” Richard Vyvyan’s own account dates the first royal messages from Glace Bay to 20–21 December 1902. Marconi stayed until mid-January 1903.

The Nobel biography dates Marconi’s first marriage to 1905. Helen’s separate recollection of visits with his wife therefore cannot simply be dated to the December 1902 letter. It could belong to later Glace Bay years or combine memories; the evidence does not settle that question.

links.title: R. N. Vyvyan, Wireless Over Thirty Years (1933)

records.title: The war years Helen meant to fill in
records.text:
Helen stops here intending to quote Frederick’s letters. His digitised service file supplies a different kind of account: an assistant-instructor appointment at the Canadian Engineers Training Depot on 29 April 1915, a short instructional visit to France that August, and a departure from Boulogne for England on 26 August. He became adjutant of the 3rd Divisional Engineers in February 1916 and transferred to the 7th Field Company that October.

The official 1925 Militia List records two periods in the combined “France and Belgium” theatre: 25 March 1916–18 March 1917 and 16 March 1918–6 May 1919. Between them, his file records a transfer to England and command of the 14th Field Company from 20 March 1917. The theatre label does not identify individual battles or prove which days he spent in each country.

In 1918 he joined the 12th Battalion, Canadian Engineers. His record also preserves a human detail—ten days’ leave to Nice granted from 21 August—and a period as acting lieutenant-colonel, 13 December 1918–10 January 1919. He sailed for Canada in June 1919 on Olympic. These are editorial additions from the records; the letters Helen intended to quote have not been found.

links.title: Service file, LAC RG 150, box 4279-18 (PDF, 36 pages)
London Gazette, 10 February 1919, page 2061: acting lieutenant-colonel

records.title: The marriage register
records.text: The Nova Scotia register confirms the marriage on 1 October 1921 at St James’ Church, Kentville, by licence. Frederick, 30, is entered as a farmer living at Blomidon, Kings County. Helen Graham, 21, was born in Toronto. Her father is George E. Graham, born in Uxbridge, Ontario. The witnesses were B. H. Henshaw of Montreal and Mary L. Graham of Kentville.

records.title: Mary Beatrice, 1922–1923
records.text: Her birth registration gives 28 August 1922 at the Westwood Hospital, Wolfville. Her father signed it as “Major F. R. Henshaw, Blomidon” and is entered as a farmer. She died at Canning on 7 April 1923 of broncho-pneumonia. She was buried at Blomidon the next day.

records.title: Assistant Director of Military Intelligence
records.text: The Department of National Defence officers’ list of July 1928 names him under the General Staff: “Assistant Director of Military Intelligence … Henshaw, Major F. R., M.C., R.C.E. … 1/1/28.” A later list gives the appointment as 1 January 1928 to 30 September 1929. The 1930 list shows his successor, his RMC classmate Kenneth Stuart, taking the post on 1 October 1929; a 1940 profile of Stuart says he edited the Canadian Defence Quarterly “from 1929 until the present war broke out.” No masthead naming the 1928–29 editor has been found, so Helen’s account of Frederick’s editing remains unconfirmed, though the post and the editorship appear to have gone together. The 1 January date is the appointment’s effective date; it does not place him physically in Ottawa before the family’s March return to Canada.

links.title: Daily Colonist, 23 August 1940, p. 2: Stuart profile

records.title: The homeward passage, 1928
records.text:
In late January 1928 the Straits Times noted Frederick’s visit to Singapore “on his way to Canada.” The Canadian passenger list shows the family on the Canadian Pacific liner Empress of Canada, sailing from Hong Kong on 15 February 1928. It lists Frederick, Helen, their daughter Helen and both sons born in Quetta. They landed at Victoria, British Columbia, on Sunday 4 March 1928. The Victoria Daily Times reported that they stayed at the Empress Hotel and left for Vancouver the next afternoon. How they travelled from Singapore to Hong Kong is not recorded.

The Hong Kong Daily Press of 16 February lists Major and Mrs F. R. Henshaw and three children among the previous day’s departures on Empress of Canada. The notice advertises the ship’s passage via Shanghai and Japan ports; it does not establish that the family went ashore. The Canadian manifest’s onward-travel column is marked C.P.R. Ferry / C.N.R., identifying intended carriers without naming a particular ferry, train or full rail itinerary.

links.title: Passenger list, Empress of Canada (LAC reel T-14889, p. 154)
Hong Kong Public Libraries: Daily Press, 16 February 1928, page 10, record NPDP19280216 (catalogue 57323)

records.title: Dates at Kingston
records.text: The 1934 Defence Forces List dates his appointment as District Engineer Officer, Military District No. 3, Kingston, from 1 October 1929 to 30 April 1933. The chapter heading uses Helen’s 1929–1932.

links.title: List of Officers, July 1932, p. 18: District Engineer Officer from 1/10/29

records.title: The published article
records.text:
The article Helen quotes is F. R. Henshaw, “To Ontario’s Sea Coast by Canoe,” Canadian Defence Quarterly 8, no. 2 (January 1931): 255–263. Contemporary indexes describe a trip from Mattice down the Missinaibi and Moose rivers to Moose Factory and James Bay. The article text itself has not yet been located online.

A contemporary abstract outlines the route from Mattice down the Missinaibi and Moose rivers to Moose Factory and James Bay, returning by the Moose and Abitibi rivers to the railhead at Coral Rapids. It supports the journey’s shape without identifying each camp or fixing the trip’s year. The 1930 RMC Review also names a separate article by Henshaw, “The Employment of Tanks,” in that April’s Defence Quarterly; the original articles are still to be located.

links.title: RMC Review, 1932: notice of the article
Canadian Historical Review, June 1931: bibliography entry
RMC Review, 1930, notice of the tank article

records.title: The engineering school at Wellington Barracks
records.text: The Canadian Military Engineers Association records that Major F. R. Henshaw was appointed the first Chief Instructor of the Royal Canadian School of Military Engineering at Halifax on 15 September 1936. This is a secondary source; it does not cite the original order.

records.title: Talavera Barracks and Pangbourne
records.text: The war diary of the 1st Canadian Division’s engineer headquarters records the 1st Field Company arriving at Talavera Barracks, Aldershot, on 10 February 1940. On 1 March “Majors Henshaw, and Kennedy” visited Wallingford and Pangbourne to prepare the bridging training held there through March.

links.title: War diary, 1 March 1940 (LAC microfilm T-18313, image 961)

records.title: The move north
records.text: The war diary dates the company’s move from Talavera Barracks to the Northampton area to 30 May 1940, not the beginning of May. That was after the 24 May episode described below. For 1 May it records an ordinary day.

records.title: Two departures in 1940
records.text: The records show two separate moves. On 24 May 1940 the company went by train to Dover for France, but the operation was cancelled and the troops disembarked. The Brittany expedition came in June. The company’s transport left for Falmouth and Brest on 8 June. The engineer headquarters party landed at Brest on 14 June, was recalled that evening, re-embarked on the Port Montreal and anchored at Falmouth on 15 June. These June pages do not name Frederick. On 21 July he was recommended to give up the 1st Field Company, become a lieutenant-colonel and command the 1st Canadian Pioneer Battalion.

links.title: C. P. Stacey, Six Years of War, chapter IX

records.title: The Senior Officers’ Course
records.text: The RMC Review of June 1942 confirms Helen’s account. Lt-Col L. T. Lowther had returned to the United Kingdom, and Lt-Col F. R. Henshaw was appointed G.S.O. 1 of the Senior Officers’ Course on 23 April 1942, having been its G.S.O. 2. Her June 1943 retirement date is still unconfirmed. His Second World War service file can be requested from Library and Archives Canada. The same issue carries a report on the courses at the College signed “F. R. H.”, almost certainly by Frederick himself; it dates the second and third courses to October–December 1941 and January–April 1942.

records.title: St Mary’s churchyard, Como
records.text: The headstone reads: “Lieut/Colonel Frederick R. Henshaw M.C., Royal Canadian Engineers, born in Montreal December 13. 1890, died Riversmead, Como, August 23. 1959.” The stroke between Lieut and Colonel is the stonemason’s mistake Helen mentions. His First World War file was later stamped “Deceased 23.8.59.” The Montreal Gazette carried the death notice on Tuesday 25 August 1959: “HENSHAW, Lieut-Col Frederick Robert. On Sun, August 23rd 1959 at Riversmead, Como. Funeral service at St Mary’s Church, Como, on Wed. August 26th at 1.30 p.m.”

links.title: Montreal Gazette, 25 August 1959, p. 29 (Google News Archive)

records.title: His identity in the official records
records.text:
Frederick’s 1916 officer’s declaration independently gives Montreal and 13 December 1890 as his birthplace and date of birth, and names his mother, Beatrice H. Henshaw of Como, as next of kin. The 1921 marriage register supplies both parents’ full names: Arthur Scott Henshaw and Beatrice Hannah Shepherd.

Lovell’s 1891–1892 Montreal directory adds the bank’s name: Arthur was a clerk at Bank of Montreal, living at 144a Durocher. The same directory places R. W. Shepherd, president of the Ottawa River Navigation Company, at 844 Dorchester. These entries corroborate the two family addresses Helen gives.

records.title: The bank and the colonel in other records
records.text:
Bank of Montreal’s own branch history dates its Glace Bay branch to 1901. This gives context for Arthur’s posting, but does not identify Heronhurst or establish where the bank-built house stood. The house remains a research gap.

Lovell’s earlier directory also places Lieutenant-Colonel F. C. Henshaw in the Victoria Rifles Armory Association. The Mount Royal monument supplies dates for the F. C. Henshaw identified in the family research as Uncle Fred: 21 July 1851–2 October 1907. His godfather role and gift of the rifle remain Helen’s family account.

links.title: Bank of Montreal, Glace Bay branch history
F. C. Henshaw memorial and monument photograph

records.title: Cadet 801
records.text: The July 1910 Militia List places Frederick Robert Henshaw among the cadets who entered RMC in 1908. His later officer’s declaration records RMC service from 1908 to 1911, and the RMC Review identifies him as No. 801. These records corroborate the college years Helen describes.

records.title: The engineers’ course in England
records.text: The April 1913 Militia List records his RCE commission dated 22 June 1911 and his secondment for instruction at the School of Military Engineering, Chatham, from 15 September 1911. The Militia Council’s report for the year ending March 1913 lists him at the School of Military Engineering in England alongside H. B. Boswell, A. G. Lawson and K. Stuart, the companions Helen names. The following year’s report again lists Henshaw, Lawson and Stuart at the school and under attachments; Boswell is no longer listed. These returns confirm the training and the colleagues; they do not date the holidays or the mess stories.

links.title: Militia Council report, year ending 31 March 1913, p. 11
Militia Council report, year ending 31 March 1914, p. 16

records.title: Defence work in the Maritime Provinces
records.text: The January 1915 Militia List names Lieutenant F. R. Henshaw as Division Officer, Maritime Provinces, with an appointment date of 9 May 1914. This records his official responsibility before he went overseas; the anecdotes about particular towns remain Helen’s own recollections.

records.title: A farmer who remained a soldier
records.text: The December 1922 Militia List places Major F. R. Henshaw with A Squadron at Canning in The King’s (Nova Scotia) Mounted Rifles. This confirms a militia role during the farming years. The official regimental name differs from Helen’s “Kings Canadian Huzzars”; her wording is preserved.

records.title: Invitation and formal appointment
records.text: The army lists distinguish the return to army life from the formal appointment. They give his RCE majority as 3 April 1924, with seniority backdated to 25 December 1922. This can coexist with Helen’s account of an invitation and work during the winter of 1923–24; the invitation is not itself an official appointment order.

records.title: A possible name for the Atlantic ship
records.text: The National Archives catalogue records Regina arriving at Liverpool from Montreal and Quebec on 29 November 1925. This matches Helen’s ports and arrival date, making Regina a strong candidate for the unnamed Atlantic liner. The passenger names have not been checked, so it is not yet a confirmed Henshaw crossing.

links.title: National Archives, Regina passenger list catalogue, BT 26/789/8

records.title: The liner’s January 1926 calls
records.text: Shipping reports place Ranpura at Port Said on 20 January, Aden on 24 January and Bombay on the morning of 29 January 1926. A contemporary report also places Lord Inchcape aboard, corroborating one of Helen’s memorable fellow passengers. These are records of the ship’s movements, not a separately checked passenger entry for the Henshaws. They leave little time for Helen’s recollection of reaching Quetta at the end of January; an exact Quetta arrival date remains unestablished.

links.title: Pinang Gazette, Lord Inchcape aboard Ranpura

records.title: Two years at Staff College
records.text: The Department of National Defence report dates Frederick’s Quetta course from February 1926 to December 1927. The Indian Army List names him among the college’s senior students. The chapter’s broader 1925–1928 span includes the journeys to India and home; it is not the duration of the course itself.

links.title: Departmental reports, 1928, National Defence, Staff College

records.title: Why he went overseas as a major
records.text: The November 1939 Defence Forces List already places him among lieutenant-colonels, with seniority dated 4 January 1938. That is important context for Helen’s statement that he would “revert to major” to command the Field Company. The July 1940 diary’s use of lieutenant-colonel should not be treated as evidence of his first promotion to that rank.

records.title: A command the biography does not name
records.text: The 1st Canadian Pioneer Battalion’s own diary records that Lieutenant-Colonel F. R. Henshaw, previously commanding the 1st Field Company, assumed command on 21 July 1940 in place of Lieutenant-Colonel J. L. Melville, and Frederick signed its pages as commanding officer. On 16 August the diary recorded the authority: “Major F. R. Henshaw, M.C., to be Lt.-Col. effective 19 Jul 40 and to command the Battalion.” His pre-war lists already gave him lieutenant-colonel’s seniority from 1938, which fits Helen’s account that he reverted to major to take the Field Company overseas and was then promoted again. The battalion was a works unit. Its diary records a move to Wentworth Hall and a job at the Mansion House, Leatherhead, in August 1940; by May 1941 it was laying drainage and water supply at Bramshott Hospital, building the Thursley and Tweedsmuir camps for Canadian Military Headquarters, and fitting a decontamination plant at Leatherhead.

Pioneer Battalion diary, August 1940: Wentworth and Leatherhead, image 956
Pioneer Battalion diary, May 1941: works, images 555–559

records.title: A year with the battalion
records.text: From Wentworth Hall, Surrey, the battalion’s companies went where the work was. In September 1940 they cleared and rebuilt the bombed Vickers-Armstrong works at Weybridge, which brought a congratulatory telegram from Lord Beaverbrook and a letter of thanks from the company’s director. Others built defence works near Brighton and at Devil’s Dyke. In December two of Frederick’s officers, Lieutenant J. M. S. Patton and Captain D. W. Cunnington, received the George Cross and George Medal for disposing of a delayed-action bomb at an aircraft factory, and the unit was renamed the 1st Battalion, Royal Canadian Engineers. Frederick signed most of the monthly diaries as commanding officer. They record him in hospital briefly in January 1941, on a course at Winterbourne Gunner in March, and inspecting work at Hythe, Shoreham and Thursley.

links.title: Diary, September 1940: Weybridge and Lord Beaverbrook’s telegram
Diary, 18 December 1940: George Cross, George Medal and new name
Diary, March 1941: course at Winterbourne Gunner

records.title: Leaving England together
records.text: The battalion’s weekly officers’ returns still list Lieutenant-Colonel Henshaw as present at the end of June 1941. The diary records him struck off strength on 4 July 1941, with a farewell party for him and Helen “on their leaving for Canada”; Major H. R. Lynn’s promotion to command is entered on 20 July. This supports Helen’s July return, though it is not a sailing or arrival date, and wartime passenger lists for 1941 are not open. The ship has not been identified.

links.title: Weekly officers’ return, week ending 28 June 1941
Diary, 20 July 1941: Major Lynn to command

records.title: Riversmead in the local record
records.text: Hudson’s municipal planning programme lists Riversmead at 245 Main among buildings of historical and architectural interest. Greenwood’s family history traces the house to Captain R. W. Shepherd and Mary Cecilia, placing their move there around 1848–1849. These sources establish the house and its earlier family connection; they do not settle when the Henshaws inherited it. That remains separate from Helen’s precise move-in date, 19 May 1944.

links.title: Hudson planning programme, appendix, printed page 22

records.title: Arthur’s injury at Almonte
records.text: A contemporary Ottawa Journal report, published 11 September 1909, describes Arthur Scott Henshaw, manager of the Bank of Montreal at Almonte, being struck by a falling telephone pole during the fire. A collapsing wall had brought down the wires and poles. Helen remembers a falling beam while he helped move possessions. Both accounts describe the same family tragedy, but the details differ. The newspaper clipping was read in a local historian’s reproduction, rather than directly through the newspaper archive.

records.title: Blomidon in the 1921 census
records.text: Enumerated at Blomidon in Cornwallis, Kings County, in early June 1921, “Henshaw, Fred” is a single man of 30, born in Quebec, living as a lodger in the household of Joseph Bennett. The entry predates the October wedding by four months.

links.title: Census of Canada 1921, Kings, Cornwallis, page 4 (LAC)

records.title: 47 George Street in the 1931 census
records.text: The 1931 census finds the family at 47 George Street, Kingston: a rented brick house of nine rooms at $75 a month. Frederick, 40, is entered as “Army Officer, R.C.E. Army.” The household is Helen, their four children, a domestic and a children’s nurse. The two boys are recorded as born in India and arriving in Canada in 1928.
